name: Meng Hao-jan
credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Meng Hao-jan (689–740) was the inseparable friend of the poet Wang Wei. He spent the first forty years of his life in study, but having failed to obtain his doctor’s degree he returned to the hills of his native province and gave his remaining years to composition.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poems.title: The Lost One
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. L. Cranmer-Byng (1909)
poems.text:
The red gleam o’er the mountains
Goes wavering from sight,
And the quiet moon enhances
The loveliness of night.

I open wide my casement
To breathe the rain-cooled air.
And mingle with the moonlight
The dark waves of my hair.

The night wind tells me secrets
Of lotus lilies blue;
And hour by hour the willows
Shake down the chiming dew.

I fain would take the zither,
By some stray fancy led;
But there are none to hear me,
And who can charm the dead?

So all my day-dreams follow
The bird that leaves the nest;
And in the night I gather
The lost one to my breast.

poems.title: A Friend Expected
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. L. Cranmer-Byng (1909)
poems.text:
Over the chain of giant peaks
The great red sun goes down,
And in the stealthy floods of night
The distant valleys drown.

Yon moon that cleaves the gloomy pines
Has freshness in her train;
Low wind, faint stream, and waterfall
Haunt me with their refrain.

The tired woodman seeks his cot
That twinkles up the hill;
And sleep has touched the wanderers
That sang the twilight still.

To-night -- ah! beauty of to-night
I need my friend to praise,
So take the lute to lure him on
Through the fragrant, dew-lit ways.

poems.title: Waiting
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Herbert A. Giles (1898)
poems.text:
The sun has sunk behind the western hill,
And darkness glides across the vale below;
Between the firs the moon shines cold and chill,
No breezes whisper to the streamlet's flow.
Belated woodsmen homeward hurry past,
Birds seek their evening refuge in the tree:
O my beloved, wilt thou come at last?
With lute, among the flowers, I wait for thee.

poems.title: In Dreamland
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Herbert A. Giles (1898)
poems.text:
The sun has set behind the western slope,
The eastern moon lies mirrored in the pool;
With streaming hair my balcony I ope,
And stretch my limbs out to enjoy the cool.
Loaded with lotus-scent the breeze sweeps by.
Clear dripping drops from tall bamboos
I hear,
I gaze upon my idle lute and sigh:
Alas no sympathetic soul is near!
And so I doze, the while before mine eyes
Dear friends of other days in dream-clad forms arise.

poems.title: At Anchor
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Herbert A. Giles (1898)
poems.text:
I steer my boat to anchor by the mist-clad river eyot,
And mourn the dying day that brings me nearer to my fate.
Across the woodland wild I see the sky lean on the trees,
While close to hand the mirrored moon floats on the shining seas.

poems.title: A Reverie in a Summer-house
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Charles Budd (1912)
poems.text:
The daylight fades behind the Western Mountains,
  And in the east is seen the rising moon,
Which faintly mirrored in the garden fountains
  Foretells that night and dreams are coming soon.

With window open--hair unloosed and flowing,
  I lie in restful ease upon my bed;
The evening breeze across the lilies blowing
  With fragrant coolness falls upon my head.

And in the solemn stillness--all-prevailing,
  The fall of dewdrops from the tall bamboos--
Which grow in graceful rows along the railing--
  Sounds through the silence soft as dove's faint coos.

On such an eve as this I would be singing,
  And playing plaintive tunes upon the lute,
And thus to mind old friends and pleasures bringing;
  But none are here to join with harp and flute!

So in a pleasant stillness I lie dreaming
  Of bygone days and trusty friends of old,
Among whom Sin-tze's happy face is beaming;
  I would my thoughts could now to him be told.

poems.title: A Night-Mooring on the Chien-te River
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
While my little boat moves on its mooring of mist,
And daylight wanes, old memories begin. . .
How wide the world was, how close the trees to heaven,
And how clear in the water the nearness of the moon!

poems.title: A Spring Morning
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
I awake light-hearted this morning of spring,
Everywhere round me the singing of birds —
But now I remember the night, the storm,
And I wonder how many blossoms were broken.

poems.title: A Message from Lake Tung-t'ing
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Here in the Eighth-month the waters of the lake
Are of a single air with heaven,
And a mist from the Yun and Mêng valleys
Has beleaguered the city of Yo-chou.
I should like to cross, but I can find no boat.
. . . How ashamed I am to be idler than you statesmen,
As I sit here and watch a fisherman casting
And emptily envy him his catch.

poems.title: On Climbing Yen Mountain with Friends
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
While worldly matters take their turn,
Ancient, modern, to and fro,
Rivers and mountains are changeless in their glory
And still to be witnessed from this trail.
. . . Where a fisher-boat dips by a waterfall,
Where the air grows colder, deep in the valley,
The monument of Yang remains;
And we have wept, reading the words,

poems.title: At a Banquet in the House of the Taoist Priest Mei
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
In my bed among the woods, grieving that spring must end,
I lifted up the curtain on a pathway of flowers,
And a flashing bluebird bade me come
To the dwelling-place of the Red Pine Genie.
. . . What a flame for his golden crucible —
Peach-trees magical with buds! —
And for holding boyhood in his face,
The rosy-flowing wine of clouds!

poems.title: On Returning at the Year's End to Chung-nan Mountain
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
I petition no more at the north palace-gate.
. . . To this tumble-down hut on Chung-nan Mountain
I was banished for my blunders, by a wise ruler.
I have been sick so long I see none of my friends.
My white hairs hasten my decline,
Like pale beams ending the old year.
Therefore I lie awake and ponder
On the pine-shadowed moonlight in my empty window.

poems.title: Stopping at a Friend's Farm-house
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Preparing me chicken and rice, old friend,
You entertain me at your farm.
We watch the green trees that circle your village
And the pale blue of outlying mountains.
We open your window over garden and field,
To talk mulberry and hemp with our cups in our hands.
. . . Wait till the Mountain Holiday —
I am coming again in chrysanthemum time.

poems.title: From Ch'in Country to the Buddhist Priest Yüan
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
How gladly I would seek a mountain
If I had enough means to live as a recluse!
For I turn at last from serving the State
To the Eastern Woods Temple and to you, my master.
. . . Like ashes of gold in a cinnamon-flame,
My youthful desires have been burnt with the years —
And tonight in the chilling sunset-wind
A cicada, singing, weighs on my heart.

poems.title: From a Mooring on the T'ung-lu to a Friend in Yang-chou
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
With monkeys whimpering on the shadowy mountain,
And the river rushing through the night,
And a wind in the leaves along both banks,
And the moon athwart my solitary sail,
I, a stranger in this inland district,
Homesick for my Yang-chou friends,
Send eastward two long streams of tears
To find the nearest touch of the sea.

poems.title: Taking Leave of Wang Wêi
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Slow and reluctant, I have waited
Day after day, till now I must go.
How sweet the road-side flowers might be
If they did not mean good-bye, old friend.
The Lords of the Realm are harsh to us
And men of affairs are not our kind.
I will turn back home, I will say no more,
I will close the gate of my old garden.

poems.title: Memories in Early Winter
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
South go the wildgeese, for leaves are now falling,
And the water is cold with a wind from the north.
I remember my home; but the Hsiang River's curves
Are walled by the clouds of this southern country.
I go forward. I weep till my tears are spent.
I see a sail in the far sky.
Where is the ferry? Will somebody tell me?
It's growing rough. It's growing dark.

poems.title: On Climbing Orchid Mountain in the Autumn
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
On a northern peak among white clouds
You have found your hermitage of peace;
And now, as I climb this mountain to see you,
High with the wildgeese flies my heart.
The quiet dusk might seem a little sad
If this autumn weather were not so brisk and clear;
I look down at the river bank, with homeward-bound villagers
Resting on the sand till the ferry returns;
There are trees at the horizon like a row of grasses
And against the river's rim an island like the moon. . .
I hope that you will come and meet me, bringing a basket of wine —
And we'll celebrate together the Mountain Holiday.

poems.title: In Summer at the South Pavilion
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
The mountain-light suddenly fails in the west,
In the east from the lake the slow moon rises.
I loosen my hair to enjoy the evening coolness
And open my window and lie down in peace.
The wind brings me odours of lotuses,
And bamboo-leaves drip with a music of dew. . . .
I would take up my lute and I would play,
But, alas, who here would understand?
And so I think of you, old friend,
O troubler of my midnight dreams!

poems.title: At the Mountain-Lodge of the Buddhist Priest Ye Waiting in Vain for My Friend Ting
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Now that the sun has set beyond the western range,
Valley after valley is shadowy and dim . . .
And now through pine-trees come the moon and the chill of evening,
And my ears feel pure with the sound of wind and water. . .
Nearly all the woodsmen have reached home,
Birds have settled on their perches in the quiet mist . . .
And still — because you promised — I am waiting for you, waiting,
Playing my lonely lute under a wayside vine.

poems.title: Returning at Night to Lu-men Mountain
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
A bell in the mountain-temple sounds the coming of night.
I hear people at the fishing-town stumble aboard the ferry,
While others follow the sand-bank to their homes along the river,
. . . I also take a boat and am bound for Lu-mên Mountain —
And soon the Lu-mên moonlight is piercing misty trees.
I have come, before I know it, upon an ancient hermitage,
The thatch door, the piney path, the solitude, the quiet,
Where a hermit lives and moves, never needing a companion.

poems.title: 訪袁拾遺不遇 (Fang yuan shi yi bu yu)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
洛陽訪才子，江嶺作流人。
聞說梅花早，何如此地春。

poems.title: 題義公禪房 (Ti yi gong chan fang)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
義公習禪寂，結宇依空林。
戶外一峯秀，階前衆壑深。
夕陽連雨足，空翠落庭陰。
看取蓮花淨，方知不染心。

poems.title: 宿建德江 (Su jian de jiang)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
移舟泊煙渚，日暮客愁新。
野曠天低樹，江清月近人。

poems.title: 春曉 (Chun xiao)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
春眠不覺曉，處處聞啼鳥。
夜來風雨聲，花落知多少。

poems.title: 宿桐廬江寄廣陵舊遊 (Su tong lu jiang ji guang ling jiu you)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
山暝聞猿愁，滄江急夜流。
風鳴兩岸葉，月照一孤舟。
建德非吾土，維揚憶舊遊。
還將兩行淚，遙寄海西頭。

poems.title: 留別王侍御維 (Liu bie wang shi yu wei)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 五言律詩. Also titled 留別王維.
poems.text:
寂寂竟何待，朝朝空自歸。
欲尋芳草去，惜與故人違。
當路誰相假，知音世所稀。
只應守寂寞，還掩故園扉。

poems.title: 早寒江上有懷 (Zao han jiang shang you huai)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 五言律詩. Also titled 早寒有懷.
poems.text:
木落雁南度，北風江上寒。
我家襄水曲，遙隔楚雲端。
鄉淚客中盡，孤帆天際看。
迷津欲有問，平海夕漫漫。

poems.title: 歲暮歸南山 (Sui mu gui nan shan)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 五言律詩. Also titled 歸故園作; 歸終南山.
poems.text:
北闕休上書，南山歸敝廬。
不才明主棄，多病故人疏。
白髮催年老，青陽逼歲除。
永懷愁不寐，鬆月夜窗虛。

poems.title: 過故人莊 (Guo gu ren zhuang)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
故人具雞黍，邀我至田家。
綠樹村邊合，青山郭外斜。
開軒面場圃，把酒話桑麻。
待到重陽日，還來就菊花。

poems.title: 秦中感秋寄遠上人 (Qin zhong gan qiu ji yuan shang ren)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 五言律詩. Also titled 秦中寄遠上人.
poems.text:
一丘常欲臥，三徑苦無資。
北土非吾願，東林懷我師。
黃金燃桂盡，壯志逐年衰。
日夕涼風至，聞蟬但益悲。

poems.title: 望洞庭湖贈張丞相 (Wang dong ting hu zeng zhang cheng xiang)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 五言律詩. Also titled 臨洞庭湖贈張丞相.
poems.text:
八月湖水平，涵虛混太清。
氣蒸雲夢澤，波撼岳陽城。
欲濟無舟楫，端居恥聖明。
坐觀垂釣者，徒有羨魚情。

poems.title: 與諸子登峴山 (Yu zhu zi deng xian shan)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
人事有代謝，往來成古今。
江山留勝蹟，我輩復登臨。
水落魚梁淺，天寒夢澤深。
羊公碑尚在，讀罷淚沾襟。

poems.title: 清明日宴梅道士房 (Qing ming ri yan mei dao shi fang)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
林臥愁春盡，開軒覽物華。
忽逢青鳥使，邀入赤松家。
金竈初開火，仙桃正發花。
童顏若可駐，何惜醉流霞。

poems.title: 秋登蘭山寄張五 (Qiu deng lan shan ji zhang wu)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 五言古詩. Also titled 九月九日峴山寄張子容.
poems.text:
北山白雲裏，隱者自怡悅。
相望試登高，心隨雁飛滅。
愁因薄暮起，興是清秋髮。
時見歸村人，沙行渡頭歇。
天邊樹若薺，江畔洲如月。
何當載酒來，共醉重陽節。

poems.title: 夏日南亭懷辛大 (Xia ri nan ting huai xin da)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
山光忽西落，池月漸東上。
散發乘夕涼，開軒臥閒敞。
荷風送香氣，竹露滴清響。
欲取鳴琴彈，恨無知音賞。
感此懷故人，中宵勞夢想。

poems.title: 宿業師山房期丁大不至 (Su ye shi shan fang qi ding da bu zhi)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 五言古詩. Also titled 宿業師山房待丁大不至.
poems.text:
夕陽度西嶺，羣壑倏已暝。
鬆月生夜涼，風泉滿清聽。
樵人歸欲盡，煙鳥棲初定。
之子期宿來，孤琴候蘿徑。

poems.title: 夜歸鹿門山歌 (Ye gui lu men shan ge)
poems.author: Meng Hao-jan
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 七言古詩. Also titled 夜歸鹿門歌.
poems.text:
山寺鐘鳴晝已昏，漁梁渡頭爭渡喧。
人隨沙岸向江村，餘亦乘舟歸鹿門。
鹿門月照開煙樹，忽到龐公棲隱處。
巖扉鬆徑長寂寥，惟有幽人自來去。
